name: GHRP-5

lead: GHRP-5 is a synthetic peptide in the growth hormone-releasing peptide family, also called the Momany peptide. People in muscle-building circles look at it for more muscle and a leaner body.

It is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor, so the idea is more GH release, higher GH and IGF-1, then more muscle and less fat. The published literature consists of anti-doping chemistry and a few laboratory studies, including one reporting that it also releases prolactin. No human clinical studies were found.

paras: It is discussed as an injectable research peptide in the same family as GHRP-1, -2, -4 and -6, usually alongside training and diet goals for muscle and leanness. Because there are no human studies, there is no established routine or timeline for results.

No human safety data were found. It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list, so it is off limits in competitive sport, and it is not an approved medicine. The laboratory prolactin finding is one more unknown.

angle.text: GHRP-5, the Momany peptide, is grouped with GHRP-1, -2, -4 and -6 as a GH-releasing peptide that bodybuilders consider for muscle and leanness. The chain people describe is GH release, higher GH and IGF-1, then more muscle and less fat; published work so far is laboratory and anti-doping literature.

lead: GHRP-5 is a synthetic growth hormone-releasing peptide, also referred to in the literature as the Momany peptide.[1] Analytical papers group it with GHRP-1, -2, -4 and -6 as synthetic met-enkephalin analogues with unnatural D-amino acids designed to stimulate growth hormone release.[2]
Published work on GHRP-5 is sparse: anti-doping chemistry, peptide-handling studies, and a laboratory study of its prolactin-releasing activity. No human clinical studies were found.

paras: GHRP-5 is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor.[3] An experimental study in Biocell reported prolactin-releasing activity of GHRP-5 on lactotroph cells in vivo and in vitro.[1] A 2026 study in Chirality examined the secondary structure, thermal stability and model-membrane interactions of GHRPs.[4]

Anti-doping laboratories have published urine screening methods covering GHRP-5, and a 2017 paper used GHRP-5 as one of four doping-relevant model peptides in a study of surface adsorption during analysis.[2][5][6] The peptides are described as orally active, and the established growth hormone test does not detect their use.[7]
